questions.enonce_markdown: With the aid of a diagram, describe the cardiac cycle. *[10 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **cardiac cycle** is the sequence of events (contraction, **systole**, and relaxation, **diastole**) which make up one heart beat. At a resting rate of about 70 beats per minute it lasts about **0.8 s**. Both sides of the heart work together; the values below are for the left side.

**Stage 1: atrial systole (about 0.1 s)**
The walls of the two atria contract, atrial pressure rises above ventricular pressure and the **atrioventricular (bicuspid and tricuspid) valves are open**, so blood is pushed into the ventricles to complete their filling. The semilunar valves are closed.

**Stage 2: ventricular systole (about 0.3 s)**
The impulse spreads from the sino-atrial node, to the atrioventricular node, the bundle of His and the Purkyne fibres, and the **ventricles contract**. Ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, so the **atrioventricular valves close** (first heart sound, "lub"). For a moment all valves are closed and pressure rises (**isovolumetric contraction**). When the ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aorta (about 16 kPa, 120 mmHg) and pulmonary artery, the **semilunar valves open** and blood is ejected into the arteries. The atria meanwhile relax and fill with blood from the venae cavae and pulmonary veins.

**Stage 3: diastole (about 0.4 s)**
The ventricles relax and their pressure falls below that in the arteries, so the **semilunar valves close** (second heart sound, "dup"), seen as a small **dicrotic notch** on the aortic pressure curve. All valves are again shut for a moment (**isovolumetric relaxation**). When ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, the **atrioventricular valves open** and blood flows passively from the atria into the ventricles (about 70 per cent of ventricular filling), until the next atrial systole begins the cycle again.

**Diagram expected (to be drawn by the candidate).** A graph with **time (s)** from 0 to 0.8 on the horizontal axis and **pressure (kPa)** on the vertical axis (0 to 16), drawn with three curves and the valve events marked:

| Curve or event | What to draw and label |
|---|---|
| Left atrium | Low curve (0.5 to 1.5 kPa) with a small bump at atrial systole |
| Left ventricle | Rises from near 0 to a peak of about 16 kPa in ventricular systole, then falls steeply to near 0 in diastole |
| Aorta | Stays between about 10.5 kPa (diastolic) and 16 kPa (systolic), with a small dip (dicrotic notch) when the semilunar valve closes |
| Marks on the time axis | (1) AV valve closes where ventricular pressure crosses above atrial; (2) semilunar valve opens where the ventricular curve crosses above the aortic curve; (3) semilunar valve closes at the dicrotic notch; (4) AV valve opens where the ventricular curve falls below the atrial curve |
| Phases below the axis | Atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, diastole 0.4 s, with the heart sounds 1 and 2 marked |

Alternatively, draw four small diagrams of the heart (atria filling, atrial systole, ventricular systole, diastole) with the position of each valve and the direction of blood flow shown by arrows.

questions.enonce_markdown: What role is played by the lymphatic system in the defense mechanisms of the body against infection? *[10 marks]* *(10, 10 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **lymphatic system** consists of **lymph capillaries and vessels** (carrying lymph), **lymph nodes**, and lymphoid organs (**spleen, thymus, tonsils, adenoids, Peyer's patches, appendix**). It plays several roles in defence against infection.

1. **Drainage of tissue fluid:** the lymph capillaries collect excess tissue fluid containing bacteria, viruses and cell debris and return it to the blood via the subclavian veins, so preventing swelling (**oedema**) and carrying pathogens to the lymph nodes for destruction. Valves in the vessels keep the lymph flowing in one direction.
2. **Filtration by the lymph nodes:** lymph flows slowly through the **lymph nodes**, where **macrophages** (phagocytes) **engulf and digest bacteria, viruses, cancer cells and debris**, so cleaning the lymph before it returns to the blood.
3. **Production and storage of lymphocytes:** lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow and mature in the **thymus** (T cells) or bone marrow (B cells), and they collect in the lymph nodes, spleen and tonsils. When a pathogen is recognised:
   - **B lymphocytes** divide to form **plasma cells** which secrete **antibodies** (humoral immunity) that bind to antigens, agglutinate and neutralise the pathogens and mark them for phagocytosis; some become **memory cells** that give a quicker, bigger response to a second infection (the basis of **immunity** and **vaccination**);
   - **T lymphocytes** (helper T cells and **killer (cytotoxic) T cells**) destroy infected body cells (**cell-mediated immunity**).
   The lymph nodes become swollen and tender in an infection because of rapid division of lymphocytes.
4. **Transport of defensive cells and antibodies:** lymph carries lymphocytes and antibodies around the body, and returns lymphocytes to the blood so they patrol all the tissues.
5. **The spleen** filters the blood, removes bacteria and old red blood cells by phagocytosis and stores lymphocytes; **tonsils and Peyer's patches** guard the entrances to the body (mouth, throat and gut) with lymphoid tissue.
6. **Lacteals** also transport absorbed fat, with the antibodies that come from the gut tissue, but this is not a defence role.
